selectedModules.name: Introduction to Molecular Life Sciences and Biotechnology

reviewedContent.CO: This course is an introduction in the field of molecular life sciences and biotechnology as well as an introduction to studying at Wageningen University. The professional field of molecular life sciences and biotechnology is very broad. You will receive an insight in the different research topics within Wageningen University, as well as several examples of the professions of several alumni. You will receive an introduction to the skills trajectory in your study programme (technical and general skills).  Several of the general skills will be introduced or expanded in this introduction course. - information literacy;  -  scientific writing skills; - presentations skills; - feedback skills; - ethics and societal aspects of biotechnology and molecular life sciences.  In profession oriented cases you will work in groups of 3 students under supervision of a mentor (senior student biotechnology or molecular life sciences).  Part of the course is given under supervision of teachers of Educational and Learning Sciences (ELS) and the University Library.

learningObjectives: Know their study programme and the professions that belong to the programme of choice
Find study related information in the course catalogue and schedule
Mention the tasks of the study advisors and know how to contact these advisors in case of any questions and problems
Critically evaluate found information and avoid plagiarism
Cite correctly and make reference lists
Write a small report
Understand that there are ethical issues associated with activities in biotechnology and molecular life sciences and the significance of them for society
Give a presentation using media and supportive non-verbal behaviour
Prepare and show structure in a presentation
Give and receive constructive feedback

selectedModules.name: General Chemistry 1

reviewedContent.AK: Chemistry at Dutch VWO level or comparable.
reviewedContent.CO: Many disciplines in the fields of life sciences, environmental sciences and technology build on concepts from physics and chemistry. The courses General Chemistry 1 and 2 intend to make you familiar with these general concepts. Among the concepts are matter and energy, size and scale, quantization of energies, driving forces, change and equilibrium. The starting point for the exploration of the various concepts is observation of the world we live in. From there, a journey is undertaken in search of the physical and chemical laws that govern the world around us. Concepts are worked out both theoretically and experimentally in tutorials and practical classes within themes and contexts from various fields. In General Chemistry 1 the emphasis is on the concepts of size and scale, probability distributions, thermal motion, Boltzmann distribution law, driving forces behind processes, equilibrium and change, adsorption, acids and bases, and kinetics of reactions.

learningObjectives: Identify aspects of the molecular motion of gases (kinetic molecular theory, collisions) and apply these to topics like the distribution of molecular speeds and the mean free path in a gas

Identify and examine driving forces (total entropy change, reaction Gibbs energy, Boltzmann distribution law) behind chemical reactions and apply these to topics like the direction of spontaneity and equilibrium constants of chemical reactions
Apply principles of reaction kinetics (reaction order, reaction rate, reaction rate law, Arrhenius equation, mechanism of a reaction) to chemical reactions
Identify properties of aqueous solutions of acids and bases and mixtures of these and apply these to topics like the pH of acidic, alkaline or buffer solutions
Explain adsorption and apply the Langmuir adsorption isotherm
Execute experiments in the domain of general and physical Chemistry following a given protocol and analyse the outcomes

selectedModules.name: Bioprocess Engineering Basics BT

reviewedContent.AK: MAT15103 Mathematics Applied: Analysis
reviewedContent.CO: This course is the first in a series of bioprocess engineering courses. It introduces the basics of design of production and transfer processes which are relevant for biotechnology. The design of the required equipment and the design of an entire biotechnological production process will be based on thermodynamic boundaries, mass and energy balances. These balances involve mathematical equations that can be applied to find the required energy and mass flows for conversion or separation processes. The emphasis in this course is on analyzing and solving relatively simple design problems to quantify the design and feasibility boundaries of a bioprocess; optimization of the design and analysis of more complex problems are taught in later courses. The course illustrates how bioprocess engineers can contribute to the development of feasible, and sustainable biotechnological production processes. *Note: This course cannot be combined in an individual program with BCT10805 Process Engineering Basics.

learningObjectives: Visualise a process in a flow sheet, using standard symbols
Explain the function and underlying mechanism of standard unit operations
Apply a systematic approach when solving design problems that are relevant for bioprocess engineers
Set up mass and energy balances that mathematically describe what goes on in a given process
Use an equilibrium design approach to evaluate the maximum performance of a process operation
Calculating the outcome of mass and energy balances at equilibrium to evaluate the performance of individual process steps
Analyse the effect of changes in individual process parameters on the performance of a biotechnological operation
Reflect on the ethical responsibilities of biotechnologists and how their worldviews shape their contributions to society and the environment

selectedModules.name: Cell Biology

reviewedContent.AK: Secondary school Biology. If this knowledge has not been obtained, please prepare by reading the first two chapters of the book: Essential Cell Biology. Keeping up with the course content is key!
reviewedContent.CO: This course is part of the first year program for Biology, Biotechnology, Molecular Life Sciences, Nutrition and Health and Plant Sciences students. The course content provides necessary knowledge for continuation courses in all these study programs. Cell Biology forms an introductory and partly specialized course into the structure and function of plant, animal and bacterial cells and biomolecules.   Special focus is directed at the ultrastructure and function of the different cell organelles, the cytoskeleton and cellular organization. Furthermore, the molecular and biochemical basis of cell function and cell differentiation processes are discussed. Recent research insights into cellular mechanisms are applied in the course. Basic principles of intra- and extracellular communication processes will be studied to obtain insight into the regulation of cell function in the context of whole tissues, organs and complete organisms. Every week has a theme and in relation to this theme there will be a practical and a group discussion. During practicals students explore, among others, mitosis and meiosis in plant and animal cells, transcriptional regulation in bacteria and the role of membranes in cell homeostasis (e.g. vacuoles, cholesterol, receptors, channels and transporters). Additionally, there is a case integrating the topics of that weeks, such as pharmaceutical compounds of plants, role of neurotransmitters in depression and regulation of cell cycles.

learningObjectives: Explain the structure and components of pro- and eukaryotic cells, especially macromolecules, cell organelles, membranes and cytoskeleton
Explain the basic principles of cellular functions: transcription, translation, replication, mitosis, meiosis and cell differentiation
Explain the basic principles of cell structure, movement and intracellular trafficking
Explain the basic principles of intra- and extra-cellular communication: receptors and signaling pathways
Explain the basic principles of light and electron microscopy
Explain the methodology of basic cell biological assays
Make slides for microscopy and interpret microscopic images effectively
Perform basic cell biological assays and interpret the obtained results
Lead a group discussion
Present a learning outcome to peers
Writing a short scientific report about an experiment

reviewedContent.CO: Genetic, physiological, morphological and ecological aspects of prokaryotes and primitive eukaryotes are addressed. The omnipresence and diversity of microorganisms is the central item.

selectedModules.name: General Chemistry 2

reviewedContent.CO: Many disciplines in the fields of life sciences, environmental sciences and technology build on concepts from physics and chemistry. The courses General Chemistry 1 and 2 intend to make you familiar with these general concepts. Among the concepts are matter and energy, size and scale, quantization of energies, driving forces, change and equilibrium. The starting point for the exploration of the various concepts is observation of the world we live in. From there, a journey is undertaken in search of the physical and chemical laws that govern the world around us. Concepts are worked out both theoretically and experimentally in tutorials and practical classes within themes and contexts from various fields. In General Chemistry 2 the emphasis is on physical and chemical properties of atoms, ions and molecules. learningObjectives: Analyse and examine aspects of chemical mass transport (friction, drift, flux, diffusion, ionic mobility) and apply these to topics like Fick’s first law, membrane potentials and electrical conductance of a solution

Analyse and examine aspects of electrochemistry (half reactions, electrochemical cells oxidation numbers, Nernst equation) and apply these to topics like spontaneity of chemical reactions, electrode potentials, equilibrium constants of electrochemical reactions and concentration measurements

Apply Lambert Beer's law and understand absorption and emission of electromagnetic radiation

selectedModules.name: Practical from Gene to Protein

reviewedContent.AK: CBI10306 Cell Biology;  MIB10306 Microbiology and Biochemistry.
reviewedContent.CO: This introductory practical course provides basic knowledge and skills to study DNA, RNA, proteins and protein function. The majority of the course consists of laboratory practical. We work in 6 themes: DNA, RNA,  Recombinant DNA technology, proteins, 3D Structure & function and protein complexes.  Lectures provide the theoretical background on these themes and the techniques used during the lab practical are also discussed in theoretical e-learning modules. The practical are dedicated to analysis of DNA, RNA and proteins, both from prokaryotes (E. coli) and eukaryotes (tomato). They include isolation of DNA, RNA and proteins, construction of a physical map of a plasmid, cloning and detection techniques like PCR and western blotting. the study of protein function and enzyme kinetics, analysis of protein 3D structure using computer graphics and the discovery of cellular protein complexes with proteomics. Students will also learn basic skills for the use of computer programs and internet tools in the analysis of structure and function of DNA and proteins (bio-informatics). Rubisco will serve as a model in the majority of the experiments. At the end of the experiments students will report about their results and conclusions. The course is concluded with an theoretical exam.  The maximal capacity for this course is limited, both in periods 4 and 5. Students for which this course is compulsory or restricted optional will be admitted with priority.

learningObjectives: Describe general genome structure and gene organisation, transcription and RNA processing in eukaryotes
Describe translation, the relation between protein structure and function and simple enzyme kinetics, regulation of enzyme activity and protein complex formation.
Understand and apply basic molecular techniques to study genes, such as restriction digestion, agarose gel electrophoresis, cloning, Southern blotting, (RT)-PCR and sequencing

Understand and apply basic techniques in biochemistry, such as protein isolation, polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, Western blotting, absorption- and fluorescence spectroscopy, immunoprecipitation and proteomics
Use DNA- and protein analysis software (BLAST, 3D-protein structure viewer, proteomics databases)
Formulate simple research questions, hypothesis and understand experimental design
Calculate and interpret independently the results of experiments and report about them in relation to the research question

selectedModules.name: Organic Chemistry 1

In the development of these processes, cellular and molecular aspects as well as process technology play a major role. The biotechnological production processes that we look into, give a broad overview of the use of biotechnology knowledge in the main different application areas (pharmaceutical, medical, food and environmental technology). The students will also gain hands-on experience in setting-up and running a bench-top bioreactor. In this practical experiment,  we will study the impact of cultivation conditions on production and growth.

selectedModules.name: Basic Cell Factory Design

reviewedContent.AK: BPE12806 Bioprocess Engineering Basics BT;  MAT15103 Applied Mathematics: Analysis;  MAT15003 Applied Mathematics: Algebra; MAT Mathematic for Biotechnology: Concepts and Methods parallel; PCC12303 General Chemistry 1.
reviewedContent.CO: Rapid advances in biology allow us to design and construct cell factories, i.e. cells which are tailored to our process. The complexity of the biochemical reaction network in a cell makes mathematical models indispensable tools for constructing, optimizing and using such cell factories. This course teaches the basic aspects of building and using bioprocess engineering models for microbial cell factories. Two types of models will be discussed: black-box models and metabolic network models. Black-box models are based on observed cell behaviour in combination with material balances. Metabolic network models are based on detailed (genomic and biochemical) knowledge of the cellular reaction network and material balances.

learningObjectives: Explain the limitations of element balances, and explain which types of models can be added
Set up and use simple network models for stoichiometric and kinetic analysis of cells
Set up and use black-box models for cells
Explain how network models and black-box models complement each other
Explain which type of model is appropriate for a certain goal
Choose experimental methods for measuring parameters for stoichiometric and kinetic models
Calculate the required parameters from experimental results

selectedModules.name: Mathematics for Biotechnology: Concepts and Methods

reviewedContent.AK: BPE12806 Bioprocess Engineering Basics;   MAT15103 Mathematics Applied: Analysis
reviewedContent.CO: In order to create a biotechnological product/service, biotechnologists meet many challenges in various fields, such as mass reactions, mass and heat transfer etc. To cope with all these aspects involved in the engineering of the production, a biotechnologist should be able to translate these challenges designing tailored mathematical models. Mathematical models are the most effective and most used tool to design, analyse and quantify the expected outcomes in large factories, avoiding expensive experimental tests and subsequently translating the results into general practical solutions. This course starts from basic principles of bioprocess engineering, mass and energy balances, as well as reaction kinetics and thermodynamic equilibrium given in Bioprocess Engineering Basics. From that point it focuses on the role of Mathematic for designing, analysing and solving problems characterised by algebraic and differential equations, with unknown variables, symbolic parameters and possible constraints. In particular, the focus will be on:  A) Identifying the complexity of the mathematical model in terms of: - the introduced variables (unknowns, coefficients, parameters and constants) - type of equations (algebraic, matrixial and differential ones) - assumptions (constraints on variables as well as on parameters)  B) Analysing and solving the model in terms of the unknown variables and studying the effect of parameter values and constraints on the solution of the problem. The theory will be applied directly to a wide variety of practical problems in biotechnology during the tutorials. We solve exercises on various topics such as Cell Factory Design, Bioreactor Design and Separation Process Design.

learningObjectives: Analyse mathematical models to solve practical problems in bioprocess engineering
Criticise the model distinguishing unknowns, coefficients, parameters and constants
Evaluate the model by solving the equations and formulating a quantitative and symbolic answer for the unknowns
Evaluate the effect of the parameter and of the assumptions on this answer within a biotechnological context

selectedModules.name: Microbial Physiology

reviewedContent.AK: Microbiology & Biochemistry
reviewedContent.CO: The Microbial Physiology course is an advanced course that addresses various aspects of microbial physiology. The following subjects are dealt with in the lectures: 1. Bioenergetics of microbial processes, 2. Respiration and fermentation, 3. Catabolic and 4. Anabolic pathways. In addition to these general aspects, various specific topics will be covered, such as pathway analysis using -omics, microbial interactions, methane formation and oxidation, bacteria and electricity, production of chemicals by microorganisms, and biofuels. Apart from the lectures the students will participate in a tutorial in which they work on theoretical assignments, including the analysis of recent scientific papers and poster preparation. The assignments guide the students to get familiar with various techniques that are common in microbial physiology research, e.g. to construct mass balances, calculate free energy changes, and look into the catabolic and anabolic pathways of diverse microorganisms. In addition, the students will take part in a practical course. In small groups (2-3 students) practical experience will be gathered by using methods and techniques that are common in microbial physiology research. The various experiments are often part of the current research of the laboratory.

learningObjectives: Explain the principles of the energy-yielding and -consuming reactions
Compose redox reactions and calculate Gibbs energy values for energy generating reactions using thermodynamic data as well as redox potentials
Explain the various catabolic and anabolic pathways and the mechanisms of energy conservation in microbial metabolism
Identify the various physiological groups of bacteria/archaea with their special features, their applications and ways to study them
Analyse recent microbial physiology related papers by working on tutorial assignments and to compose concise and accurate answers
Execute various analyses/experiments commonly involved in microbial physiology research and interpret and describe the results concisely

Understand spectroscopic theory and use this to solve problems
Apply (theoretically and practically) various extraction, sample clean-up, and chromatographic techniques to separate compounds
Appraise published analytical procedures and explain the logic behind them
Apply sample preparation and spectroscopic techniques to obtain spectra from compounds
Interpret recorded spectra and propose a chemical structure based on those data
Prepare and have an oral discussion on the chromatography practical sessions
Prepare a written spectroscopy report that summarises and discusses collected data in a clear fashion

selectedModules.name: Protein Biochemistry

reviewedContent.AK: BIC10306 Practical From Gene to Protein MIB10306 Microbiology & Biochemistry ORC12803 Organic Chemistry 1 ORC12903 Organic Chemistry 2
reviewedContent.CO: **Please note that this is a course with a limit amount of spaces - please register before the registration deadline!**   The course Protein Biochemistry is comprised of two modules: 1-Biocatalysis (16 lectures and 3 (BYOD) tutorials); 2-Purification strategies (two week full-time practical course, including 3 central and 7 decentralized lectures).   1) Biocatalysis   The most important principles in (bio)catalysis are reviewed in 16 lectures. Within the lectures, the following subjects are covered:  -Reaction kinetics, acid-base, nucleophilic, and metal-ion catalysis, protein structure, catalytic strategies of enzymes, enzyme kinetics, cofactor-dependent catalysis, enzyme inhibition, and regulation of enzyme activity.  The theory is further practiced in three tutorials, one of which is a BYOD tutorial which covers enzyme kinetics.   The Biocatalysis module is concluded with an exam (50% of final grade; minimum grade 5.50).   2) Purification strategies  Experimental characterization of proteins, including enzyme activity, requires a very pure protein sample. In the purification strategies module, the theory behind purification of enzymes from cells or tissues is covered in seven lectures. During the (full-time) practical course, groups of 2-3 students purify two enzymes using various purification strategies, including precipitation methods and different (automated) chromatography techniques (ion-exchange chromatography, affinity chromatography, hydrophobic interaction chromatography, and size exclusion chromatography). Furthermore, characterization of the purified enzymes is performed. This includes performing (kinetic) enzyme activity assays and calculating enzyme activity. Students record their results in a lab journal.   The performance of the students during the practical course and the results obtained during the practical course and recorded in a lab journal are graded (each 12. 5% of final grade; minimum grade 5.50)   The purification strategies module is concluded with an exam (25% of final grade; minimum grade 5.50)  Examination The final grade for Protein Biochemistry is composed of the following partial grades: 1) a grade for the exam on the Biocatalysis module -Open questions | 50% of the final grade; minimum grade 5.50 2) a grade for performance and results obtained during the Purification strategies module  -Personal evaluation of performance (12.5% of final grade) and lab journal describing methods and results (made with group of 2-3 students; 12.5% of final grade) | Combined 25% of final grade; minimum grade 5.50 3) a grade for the test on the theory from the Purification strategies module -Open questions | 25% of the final grade; minimum grade 5.50  **Please note that partial grades remain valid until the end of the academic year following the academic year in which the results were attained - after that all partial grades expire**

learningObjectives: Describe the basic chemical principles that underlie the enzymatic catalysis and perform related calculations
Explain how enzymes catalyze chemical reactions and discuss what factors can influence enzyme activity
Use experimentally obtained results of chemical and enzymatic reactions to calculate kinetic parameters of the reaction
Classify enzymes based on their structural features and explain how these features influence their catalytic properties
Execute proper handling and purification of proteins in a laboratory setting
Perform enzymatic assays and use experimentally obtained results to calculate specific activity and yield
Given the physico-chemical properties of a protein, design a multi-step purification method that can be used to purify that protein

selectedModules.name: Cell Physiology and Genetics

reviewedContent.CO: Cell Physiology and Genetics gives an integrating view of genetics, biochemistry and molecular biology. Background knowledge in each field is presented in the context of selected cases. Each case is approached from a genetic, molecular biological and a biochemical perspective, and is further deepened by discussing relevant research papers. Selected cases (that can be due to change) are: 'Sickle Cell Disease', 'Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy', ' Chromatin structure and function', 'Auxin Signal Transduction' and 'p53 and Cancer'.

learningObjectives: Explain the basic principles of inheritance of genetic information, and of mechanisms creating genetic diversity (gene and chromosome mutation, recombination processes)
Explain how chromosomes and chromatin are organised and how genetic information is mapped
Infer the complex relation between genotype and phenotype
Describe the principles of expression of genetic information by transcription and translation and of the regulatory mechanisms occurring in these processes
Describe the folding, distribution, modification and degradation of proteins, and how their function relates to their structure
Infer the importance of these regulatory mechanisms for a variety of fundamental processes in living organisms, like creation of diversity, development, cell differentiation, metabolism, disease

Explain how to use experimental approaches such as yeast two-hybrid, fluorescent in situ hybridization, micro arrays, reporter genes, affinity purification, mass spectrometry, pedigree analysis, chromatin immuno-precipitation

selectedModules.name: Separation Process Design

reviewedContent.AK: BPE12806 Bioprocess Engineering Basics BT;  BPE38306 Bioreactor Design; BPE22306 Basic Cell Factory Design; MAT15103 Mathematics Applied: Analysis;  MAT15203 Mathematics Applied: Algebra;  PCC12303 General Chemistry 1;  PCC12403 General Chemistry 2. MATMathematics for Biotechnology: Concepts and methods
reviewedContent.CO: Separating desired biological molecules from undesired by-products or feedstock residues is very important in the bioprocess industry and in biorefineries. It often requires separation of particles such as cells, organelles or product crystals from liquids, using sedimentation tanks, centrifuges or (membrane) filters. Separation of desired molecules from undesired ones is also frequently required, using for example extraction, adsorption, crystallization or evaporation. Finally it may be necessary to add or remove heat. This course teaches you how to design such separation units following either an equilibrium based approach or a transport rate-based approach; it extends the theory from BPE-12806 which uses only equilibria. You will learn how to derive the algebraic equations or ordinary differential equations needed for the unit design from force, mass and energy balances, and how to use them to calculate the required size, the allowed feeding rate or the possible product recovery efficiency of a separator. Attention is also paid to the design of simple process involving coupled process unit operation.  This course is part of a series of process engineering courses, so skills and knowledge from BPE-12806 are required, as well as skills and knowledge from 1st-year mathematics and physical chemistry courses. Simple concepts of bioprocess engineering design are assumed to be known to set mass and energy balances and to evaluate the performance of unit operations. Knowledge of methods for solving linear and non linear algebraical equation system as well as ordinary differential equation systems is mandatory. Knowledge of physics of fluid and granular solids are required.

learningObjectives: Identify the rate-affecting phenomena in separators discussed in the course
Select the best approach to design the operation between a rate- and an equilibrium-based- set up the balance equations required for the design of a separator, analyse and solve them
Identify the degrees of freedom in the design of a separator and explain their effect
Evaluate the consequences of design choices, also in combinations of separators
Optimise the operation of a separator, selecting the most appropriate performance criterion

selectedModules.name: Gene Technology

reviewedContent.AK: BIC10306 Practical From Gene to Protein and either BIC20306 Cell Physiology and Genetics or GEN11806 Fundamentals of Genetics and Molecular Biology.
reviewedContent.CO: Recombinant DNA technology has brought about a revolution in our understanding of molecular processes in living organisms. To date, there is no field in experimental biology that has remained untouched by the potential of isolating, analyzing and manipulating genes and organisms. Thus, gene technology provides essential tools in both fundamental and applied medical, industrial, agricultural, environmental and biological research. In this course we will focus on four major topics, including (i) production of transgenic mammals, (ii) altering gene function using knockouts, RNAi and gene editing, (iii) transgenic mice as human model systems and (iv) production of transgenic crops. In addition to conventional lectures that will outline the major procedures, applications and some research papers, students will be challenged by virtual (computer based) experimental designs on the generation and characterization of transgenic animals and plants. The practical course involves biomolecular techniques to illustrate two experiments.The first one will deal with the identification, characterization and complementation of mutations in organisms. Basic and more advanced gene technology will be applied such as genomic and plasmid DNA isolation, PCR, golden gate cloning, transformation, restriction/digestion and complementation analysis. The second experiment centers on the generation of site specific mutations and gene editing using CRISPR-Cas technology. These experiments will be supported in a virtual environment. Due to a limited number of places available in the practical part of the course, students are encouraged to register in time. Students for which this course is compulsory or restricted optional take precedence.

learningObjectives: Explain methods currently used to clone, analyse and edit genes and to introduce foreign genes into animals and plants
Design experimental strategies and interpret experimental data involving gene technology (in silico)
Apply basic recombinant DNA techniques
Interpret results from experiments involving recombinant DNA techniques
Incorporate results in a written report
Apply basic regulations when working with genetically modified micro-organisms

selectedModules.name: Communication and Technology

reviewedContent.CO: This intensive course provides insights into theoretical and practical-matters of strategic communication about novel technologies and their application in society, i.e. novel products such as foods or medical services. Special attention will be given to the life sciences and life-science technologies such as biotechnology, genomics and (bio-)nanotechnology. In our rapidly changing knowledge society, experts, and non-experts tend to have different appreciations of science and technology issues. What exactly is the nature of these differences and what are the communicative implications? How does communication affect the perception of novel technologies, their risks and benefits? How do people process complex information regarding particular risks and what is the role of emotions therein? How does media coverage of risks affect the public sense of anxiety? What is the role of trust in communication about novel technologies and how is trust built or undermined? The course will introduce relevant perspectives from innovation theory, social psychology, and sociology. Working in small groups, students will analyse the communication issues around specific technological innovations of their choice, conduct focus group research, and develop a communication plan. Feedback on weekly assignments and group work will help students to translate theoretical insights into their own applied communication strategy.

learningObjectives: Explain the importance of communication in and for (your future) professional practice in (bio-) technology
Identify factors , from scientific literature, that determine whether or not people accept and use biotechnological inventions
Describe how knowledge, attitudes, social influences, risk perceptions, and media attention can shape people's willingness to accept biotechnology and its applications
Identify several communication techniques to influence knowledge, attitudes, social influences and risk perceptions and thereby biotech acceptance
Describe the potential influence of communication messages through various channels (i.e., individual, group, media)
Obtain insight into the acceptance of a particular biotechnological invention by organising a small focus group discussion
Apply knowledge about when and how to strategically communicate in order to increase the chance that people will accept and use biotech inventions
Design a simple communication strategy that targets determinants of biotechnology adoption

selectedModules.name: Biotechnology 2

reviewedContent.AK: BPE38306 Bioreactor Design MIB20306 Microbial Physiology BIC20806 Protein Biochemistry    MOB20306 Gene Technology
reviewedContent.CO: Several steps are necessary to develop a new biotechnological application. Various aspects have to be taken into consideration: research and development, production methods, safety aspects, sales, distribution and administration. Thus, not only technical aspects determine whether the introduction of a new biotechnological process will become a success. In addition to the technical aspects patents, GMP, ISO, safety, marketing and law have to be considered. Using established production processes, this course shows how technical and economic factors interact during the introduction of a new product or process. The first part of the course focuses on known process developments. During the second part, students have to develop a new hygienic process (step) or product and reflect on possibilities for innovation.

learningObjectives: Name and describe important technical and economic factors during the introduction of a new biotechnological process
Judge whether a process or product has the potential to become patented
Judge whether a process step or chosen micro-organism will be safe
Predict arguments based on marketing reasons
Predict arguments based on laws and national or international standards
Evaluate the hygienic design of a current biotechnological process
Write a short report on biotechnological research or design
Reflect on social or ethical issues related to a biotechnological application or development
Reflect on innovation related to a biotechnological process or product

reviewedContent.CO: Building on an understanding of (simple) models, implications of model assumptions, interpretation of parameters; checking model assumptions; testing hypotheses for population means, for the 1-sample and 2-samples situations, for independent normal data (t-test); construction of a confidence interval for a population mean, or difference in means; simple linear regression and correlation, estimation, hypothesis testing and construction of a confidence interval for intercept, slope and predictions. Determine the appropriate statistical procedure, given the description of the experiment, the research question and the type of data
Apply a hypothesis test for a (difference of) population mean(s), intercept or slope (t-test)
Construct a confidence interval for a (difference of) population mean(s), intercept, slope and predictions
Show understanding of the implications of model assumptions
Apply checks for model assumptions

selectedModules.name: Modelling Dynamic Systems

reviewedContent.AK: BPE10305 Process Engineering Basics
reviewedContent.CO: In this course you will learn how to describe and how to model the time-dependent behaviour of various (bio-)chemical, thermal, and mechanical systems and processes. The modelling starts with the development of mathematical models based on mass and energy balances, mechanics or the kinetics of chemical and biological reactions. The approach is generic and can be applied to all kind of systems, such as the growth of plants and microorganisms, biological and chemical reactions in bioreactors, greenhouses, food processing, and to biological systems. These models are important for answering research questions about the time behaviour of these processes and for (re)designing a system. The course starts with the translation of oral and written problems into a mathematical model by organizing the information in sketch, diagram or drawing. Next the non-steady state balances for this system are formulated using scientific knowledge and measurement data. Furthermore you will learn how to solve the mathematical model and to analyse the dynamic behaviour of the modelled system. Several techniques, methods and model representations will be used to represent and analyse the dynamic systems. Once a model is formulated for a system, the model needs to be verified with experimental data. Techniques and limitations of methods to fit the models to data are discussed and exercised. The methods learned in the course will be demonstrated by discussing several application examples in the lectures and by a practical for simulation and analysis.

learningObjectives: Create a mathematical systems model from an oral or written problem description of a simple system (0-d, well-mixed) through application of scientific knowledge and measurement data
Translate mathematical systems models into differential equation models and to solve and analyse these models
Understand and recognise the different types of variables of a systems model written in state-space form
Approximate non-linear systems by linearised systems
Determine and compute system behaviour, equilibriums, and system properties such as stability
Represent elementary linear systems by means of a state-space model and convert one into the other
Apply parameter estimation to estimate unknown parameters of a mathematical systems model in state-space form

selectedModules.name: Mathematics for Time-dependent Systems

reviewedContent.AK: MAT15103 Mathematics Applied: Analysis and MAT15203 Mathematics Applied: Linear Algebra.
reviewedContent.CO: The study of (bio)technological systems requires mathematical and systems knowledge for analysis and interpretation of the behavior. In this course, the basic concepts that reveal the behavior of systems as gene networks, cell fluxes and bioreactors are discussed. The course is based on a systems approach for defining subunits of the systems and uses differential equations to find the time behavior of the systems. Matrix calculus that supports these techniques and methods for the interpretation of results and data obtained from experiments are discussed. The practicals contain simulation exercises to solve the differential equations numerically and to interpret the results and experimental data.

learningObjectives: Apply algebraic solution methods to solve (systems of) differential equations and apply numerical methods to approximate solutions to (systems of) differential equations, both by hand and using mathematical software.
Analyse problems in biology, biotechnology and agrotechnology, and use modelling techniques to represent these problems mathematically as (systems of) differential equations.
Interpret mathematical models in the context of (systems of) differential equations, and assess mathematical results in relation to the underlying problems.

selectedModules.name: General Safety

reviewedContent.CO: At WUR we value your safety. Therefore many measures are taken in order to facilitate a safe study in Wageningen. And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures. Therefore the General Safety course is mandatory for all new students at WUR. This course will introduce you to safety at Wageningen University & Research. We'll cover a broad range of topics to prepare you for a safe stay at our university:      in case of emergency: how to respond to emergencies;    computer work: how to prevent complaints on arms, neck and shoulder (CANS/ RSI);    social safety and being an active bystander.

learningObjectives: Have a basic understanding on how safety is managed at WUR
Know the difference between risks and hazards
Report accidents and incidents
Know which general rules apply regarding safety at WUR
Know which factors contribute to an ergonomic workspace
Adjust the computer workspace to work ergonomically correct
Know how to act as an active bystander
Know how to give and ask for consent in social engagements
Know where to seek help

selectedModules.name: Laboratory Safety

reviewedContent.CO: At WUR we value your safety. Working in a laboratory environment exposes you to specific risks: you work with (very) harmful substances that can cause serious injury or even death when not handled properly. Therefore many measures are taken in order to facilitate the safety of all present in laboratoria, from mandatory laboratory coats and a ban on eating and drinking to safe working guidelines. And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures. Therefore the Laboratory Safety course is mandatory for all students working in a laboratory environment.  In this course you'll be introduced to working safe in the laboratories of WUR and cover a range of topics for working in our biological and chemical laboratories:     General safety while working in the lab    Hazardous substances/ chemicals    Biological agents

learningObjectives: Know which basic rules apply to working in a biological or chemical laboratory
Be aware of the urgency of proper chemical and biological waste disposal
Know where to find the required information for chemical and biological waste disposal
Find safety information for chemicals used by using safety symbols, H and P sentences and the MSDS
Know how to use the safety and personal protective equipment available
